column1: On the piano keyboard, how do you locate C and F by feel alone, without looking?
column2: C is the white key immediately left of the two-black-key group; F is the white key immediately left of the three-black-key group.

column1: Why are black keys raised ~13mm above and set back from white keys?
column2: It matches the natural arc of a relaxed hand: fingertips rest on white keys while fingerpads reach black keys without lifting the wrist, preventing tension injuries.

column1: What anatomical structure causes the 'Ring Finger Problem' where finger 4 drags on 3 and 5?
column2: The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) — fingers 2-5 share one deep flexor muscle belly, so pulling finger 4 drags on the tendons of 3 and 5.

column1: Why do passages built on fingers 1-2-5 feel easier than passages built on 3-4?
column2: Fingers 1 and 5 have dedicated extensor muscles (extensor indicis, extensor digiti minimi) giving partial independence for free, while 3 and 4 are linked by extensor crosstalk (juncturae tendinum).

column1: Why does a curved finger produce more efficient, stable key control than a flat finger?
column2: As a third-class lever, a curved finger routes pulling force straight down through the bone column into the key; a flat finger bends force sideways at the last joint, forcing unnecessary stabilizer co-contraction.

column1: What interval stacking produces a major triad, and how does it relate to the overtone series?
column2: A major third (4 semitones) stacked under a minor third (3 semitones) = major chord; this mirrors the natural overtone series stack (octave, fifth, octave, major third), making it sound inherently complete.

column1: What interval stacking produces a diminished triad, and why is it unstable?
column2: Two minor thirds stacked (e.g., B-D-F); the outer notes form a tritone (exact half-octave), the most unstable interval, demanding resolution (as in vii°).

column1: Why does the G major triad use 1-2-5 fingering instead of 1-3-5?
column2: B and D are only a minor third apart with no black key between B and C; 1-3-5 crushes fingers together. Using finger 2 on B creates a natural arch, freeing finger 5 for D.

column1: What is 'escapement' in piano key mechanics, and why does pressing harder after key-bottom do nothing?
column2: Escapement releases the hammer into free flight toward the string at roughly 2-3mm (or ~10mm key depth, depending on source) before/at key bottom; once released, the hammer is ballistic and no further finger force can change its velocity or the resulting tone.

column1: What happens if a pianist's finger decelerates before reaching the escapement point?
column2: The hammer loses velocity before release, producing a soft or non-sounding note regardless of intended dynamic — tentative playing sounds weak even if marked forte.

column1: What effect occurs when two hands commit through the escapement point with matched vs. mismatched timing?
column2: Matched timing produces a fused, percussive attack (good for block chords/unison); a 20-30ms lag between hands produces a smeared, arpeggiated effect.

column1: What is the approximate physical span of one octave (thumb to pinky, 8 white keys), and what does it imply about hand position?
column2: About 164mm; most adult hands can cover this with a relaxed span — if the palm flattens or wrist lifts to reach it, the hand position is wrong, not the hand size.
